r: During the colonial time period (1619-1776), black slaves were primarily imported from West Africa to work on plantations in the Caribbean, North and South America. The transatlantic slave trade caused an immensely devastating impact on African cultures and societies and was a major cause of the African American descendancy. Black slaves were also employed in other industries such as mines, textile mills, and household service. As the United States formed, many colonists, especially those in the south relied heavily on slave labor for economic growth. In 1792, the first non-native American to become a US President, George Washington, signed the Slave Trade Act, which limited the international slave trade but didn’t outlaw it completely. The act only forbade the importation of enslaved Africans. This limited the importation of African slaves to 8788 people, 3.2% of whom were freed by owners. The southern United States had the highest percentage of enslaved Africans during this period. The number of African American slaves in the 1860 US population census was roughly 3.5 million, out of a total of 12 million people in the US. After the US civil war, African American emancipation was granted in 1865 and later in 1870, slavery was abolished altogether in the United States through the 13th Amendment. After this, many of the ex-slaves gained citizenship and fought for more rights and equal opportunities in the Jim Crow era that followed.  Although laws to ensure equality and justice for blacks were implemented, racism and discrimination persists in the United States to this day.
